1: Lectures eleven and twelve: multivariate analysis. We cover multicollinearity, the variance inflation factor, and discovering groups with clustering, specifically K means, and how to interpret the clusters.
2: What changes when we add more features? So far we compared features two at a time. But real datasets rarely explain themselves through a single pair. Patterns often appear only when several features are considered together. This brings two ideas. First, redundant features: two or more features can carry almost the same information, wasting model capacity and distorting results. This is multicollinearity. Second, hidden groupings: records can form natural groups across several features at once, invisible in any single scatterplot. This is what clustering finds.
3: Multicollinearity is when one feature can be predicted with high accuracy from a combination of the other features, meaning it adds little independent information. Why does it matter? It distorts distance based methods like clustering, inflates the importance of a repeated signal, and makes results harder to interpret. A pairwise check is not enough: two features can look uncorrelated with each other individually, yet still be predictable from a combination of several other features together. So we need a measure that looks at each feature against all the others combined, and that is exactly what V I F does.
4: V I F, the variance inflation factor. For each feature, V I F fits a mini regression predicting that feature from all the other features, and asks how much of its variance is explained by the rest. The formula is V I F equals one divided by one minus R squared, where R squared comes from regressing this one feature on every other feature. A high R squared, meaning the others predict this one well, gives a high V I F, so the feature is redundant. Interpretation: a V I F of one means no correlation with other features. One to five is moderate and generally acceptable. Five to ten is high and worth investigating. Above ten is severe multicollinearity, so consider dropping the feature.
5: Now a question about rows, not columns. Once we have confirmed the features are independent enough to trust, we can ask: do orders naturally cluster into distinct kinds, without us telling the data what those kinds should be? In supervised learning we already know the labels, like category, and try to predict them. In unsupervised learning, or clustering, no labels exist, and the algorithm groups records purely by how similar they are across features.
6: An introduction to clustering, for exploratory purposes only. No labels are given to the algorithm. It discovers structure using only how similar records are across the numeric features. We use it here purely to explore: does structure exist, and if so, what distinguishes each group? We are not building a predictive model or classifying new incoming orders, just describing the data we already have.
7: How does K means find groups? Five steps. One, choose k, the number of groups, called centres, to look for. Two, place the k centres, initially at random, in the feature space. Three, assign: every record joins the nearest centre, forming k groups. Four, update: each centre moves to the average position of its group. Five, repeat steps three and four until the assignments stop changing. In this course we run K means only to describe existing data. The found groups summarise patterns, and they do not predict labels for new records.
8: Before clustering, scale the features. K means measures how far apart two records are. If features are on very different scales, the largest scale feature silently dominates that distance, and the algorithm ends up clustering on that one feature alone. Sales ranges from zero to twenty two thousand six hundred thirty eight dollars and would dominate. Discount ranges from zero to point eight and would barely register. The fix is standard scaler, which rescales every feature to mean zero and standard deviation one, so sales, quantity, discount and profit all count equally.
9: How many groups? K means needs k decided in advance. The silhouette score helps judge a choice of k. For each point, it compares how close it is to its own cluster versus the nearest other cluster. It ranges from minus one, poor separation, through zero, ambiguous, to plus one, strong separation. The scores are point five oh four for k equals two, point four seven three for three, point four three one for four, point four three seven for five, and point three eight for six. K equals two scores highest, but it only splits orders into smaller versus larger. K equals three is a close second and yields three clearly interpretable business groups. The statistically best k is not always the most useful one.
10: Seeing the clusters. A scatterplot with hue equals cluster colours each point by its assigned group, a quick check that the clusters correspond to a visible pattern. A pairplot with hue equals cluster shows every pair of features at once, each coloured by cluster, the fastest way to see separation across all dimensions together.
11: Giving the groups a business meaning. A cluster number means nothing on its own. Interpretation reuses the grouped statistics pattern from bivariate analysis, with group by cluster instead of group by an existing category. Cluster zero has six thousand nine hundred nine orders, average sales one twenty two dollars, discount point one, profit about twenty one dollars: everyday orders. Cluster one has one thousand sixty eight orders with an average discount of point six six and average profit of minus one hundred six dollars: heavy discount, loss making. Cluster two has two thousand seventeen orders, average sales six hundred thirty four dollars and profit one twenty eight dollars: high value, high profit. Cluster one is the standout finding: heavy discounting is wiping out profit entirely, turning into a hypothesis worth testing formally: is this discount policy destroying value? As a sanity check, cross tabulate clusters against an existing category like product category to confirm the groups make real world sense.
12: What K means does not tell you. One, it is not a prediction model: in this course clustering is exploratory only, describing existing records and not classifying new orders. Two, k is chosen, not discovered: silhouette helps compare candidate values, but does not reveal a single correct number. Three, it is sensitive to scale and outliers: unscaled features or a few extreme values can distort the groups, so always scale first and check for outliers. Four, clusters need a sanity check: a statistically tight cluster is only useful if it also makes business sense, so always interpret with grouped statistics and domain knowledge.
13: Key takeaways. Multivariate analysis studies several features together, not just one or two at a time. Multicollinearity means a feature is largely redundant given the others, checked with correlation and, more rigorously, with V I F. V I F near one is ideal, above five is worth investigating, and above ten is severe. K means discovers groups in records with no labels, used here for exploration, not prediction. Always scale features before K means so no single feature dominates the distance. The silhouette score helps compare values of k, but the highest score is not always the most useful. And a cluster only becomes meaningful once interpreted with grouped statistics and sanity checked against known categories.
